rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions and comments! Please see our detailed responses below:

1. "This dataset is licensed for noncommerical use, which is suboptimal relative to some other RAG datasets, like FreshLLM, which seem to be licensed for commercial use (under the Apache license)."
- Thank you a lot for the suggestion! We will reach out to our company’s legal team to investigate the possibility of using a commercial use license.  

2. "I would have liked to see more open source models tested (the only open weights model evaluated is Llama 3 instruct)."
- Thank you for your valuable comment on expanding the scope of the experiment! In light of your suggestion, we added experiments for three popular open source models: Mixtral, Falcon and FLAN-T5. Please see the result in Table 11 attached. We used the same context length for the Mixtral model (4k tokens from web + 2k tokens from mock kg). For Falcon and FLAN-T5, we used shorter context lengths (1k tokens from web + 0.5k tokens from mock kg), as these two models tend to show unstable or suboptimal behavior with long contexts. Also, we only provided the latency numbers for models using the same context sizes to provide a fair comparison.

3. "It was not clear whether the human annotator instructions have been released, as well as the prompts/instruction for automated evaluation, but it would be great to have all those instructions released as part of the dataset."
- Thank you for the suggestion! We will add the human annotation instructions to the revised paper. 
- We released a prompt for the auto-eval that is similar to [the prompt](https://gitlab.aicrowd.com/aicrowd/challenges/meta-comprehensive-rag-benchmark-kdd-cup-2024/meta-comphrehensive-rag-benchmark-starter-kit/-/blob/master/prompts/templates.py?ref_type=heads) we were using during the KDD Cup . We didn’t release the exact version to avoid prompt attack during the competition. We will add the released prompt to the Appendix in the next version of the paper.

4. "Finally, no framework is provided to evaluate the effects of instruction fine-tuning or other type of fine-tuning of the RAG models. I would have liked to see more details about that potential direction (e.g., can the dataset be leverage for fine-tuning)."
- The CRAG benchmark can be utilized for fine-tuning. As mentioned in Section 4.2, the CRAG dataset is split into validation set, public test set, and private test set with a ratio of 3:3:4. Users can utilize the validation set to fine-tune their models and test the fine-tuned models on the public test set. 
- We will clarify this in the next version of the paper.

5. "Section 1 refers to the 3 tasks as web retrieval, structured querying and summarization while Section 2 refers to them as retrieval summarization, KG and web retrieval augmentation and end-to-end RAG. It would be easier to follow the paper if the tasks are named consistently."
- Thank you for pointing out this naming inconsistency! We will align the naming of the tasks in the revised paper.

6. "For the closed models tested, I suggest providing the dates when the relevant API's were called."
- Below are the dates when we called each industry SOTA RAG systems:
    - Copilot Pro: 2024-05-12 ~ 2024-05-16;
    - Gemini Advanced: 2024-05-20 ~ 2024-05-28;
    - ChatGPT Plus: 2024-05-27 ~ 2024-06-02;
    - Perplexity.ai: 2024-05-15 ~ 2024-05-16.
    
    All timezones are in Pacific Time (PT). Moreover, the version of ChatGPT we used in our model-based automatic evaluation is gpt-3.5-turbo-0125. The version of GPT-4 Turbo used in our baselines is gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09. 
- We will add these details to the revision. 

7. "Overall, the relation to other datasets relevant to RAG is adequately discussed. I would have liked to understand how this benchmark is different from the RAG TREC (https://trec-rag.github.io) which uses modified MS Marco corpus."
- Thank you for pointing out this related work. The TREC RAG benchmark is more recent than ours, and its competition has not yet concluded. We summarize the key differences between the TREC benchmark and CRAG based on the current information as follows:
    - The TREC RAG benchmark does not provide content from  Knowledge Graphs (KGs), making it more focused on evaluating web-based RAG solutions, CRAG supports integrating both web (through retrieved web content) and KG (through mock APIs) information. 
    - CRAG defines questions with different popularity (head, torso, and tail) and dynamisms (static, slow-changing, fast-changing, and real-time) explicitly. Besides, while TREC RAG focuses on complex questions with long answers, CRAG covers simple as well as complex question types. These three types of fine-grained information are crucial for researchers to comprehensively understand the strengths and weaknesses of their developed solutions.
    - TREC RAG assesses a RAG system's ability to retrieve information from a large collection of documents. In contrast, CRAG also evaluates the scenario of non-perfect coverage (with only 5 pages in Task 1), allowing us to test whether the RAG solutions admit "I don't know" when the retrieval results do not contain the necessary information.

8. "The dataset is currently hosted on AICrowd and the authors state their intention to host it long-term in a Meta Research Github repo. In principle the Github (and AICrowd?) repos may be permanently deleted by Meta. Hosting the dataset in a permanent repository, like zenodo, would provide stronger assurances of long-term preservation."
- Thank you for the suggestion! While we currently plan to host the dataset on AICrowd and a Meta Research Github repo, we understand the potential risks associated with platform changes. To mitigate this, we will reach out to our company's legal team for hosting the dataset in a permanent repository like Zenodo.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions and comments! And we are very glad to hear the reviewer finds "CRAG addresses a current gap in RAG research". Below are our detailed responses:

1. "CRAG only benchmark the generative model in the process, and leave the retrieval part not fully covered (Although end-to-end RAG task require the entire system), but it does not provide a way to benchmark the quality of the retriever."
- We will make it clearer that none of the three tasks we designed are for independently evaluating the quality of the retriever. This design choice was made to ensure that the competition is both challenging and manageable within a 3-month timeframe, as required by KDD Cup.
- With that being said, **the users of our dataset can choose to take the union of all 220K web pages as a corpus and build a retriever over it.** Though not comparable w. the whole web, this corpus allows fair comparison and manageable cost.
- We will make the above clear in the next version of the paper.

2. "The benchmark relies on static snapshots of data for evaluation, which may not fully account for the constantly changing nature of information, particularly for real-time and fast-changing facts."
- We collected snapshots of the KG and web search data concurrently with posing the real-time and fast-changing questions. This ensures that we capture the "snapshot" of the information world at the question-answering time. A RAG solution that works well on the benchmark should also be able to handle reasoning over time and generalize to changing questions in general.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions and comments!

1. "The benchmark uses a small retrieval candidate pool (up to 50 web pages per question). It does not directly evaluate a first-stage candidate pool construction, which is a challenging retrieval task in its own right. The benchmark should be clearer that it is not providing an end-to-end evaluation of RAG systems, e.g. in situations where Google is not available."
- The three tasks in our benchmark do not directly evaluate a first-stage candidate pool construction. This design choice was made to ensure that the competition is both challenging and manageable within a 3-month timeframe, as required by KDD Cup.
- With that being said, the users of our dataset can choose to take the union of all 220K web pages as a corpus and build a retriever over it. Though not comparable w. the whole web, this corpus allows fair comparison and manageable cost.
- We will make the above clear in the revised paper. 

2. "The paper lacks a clear description of the validation process for question/answer pairs. While some manual verification is mentioned, the methodology for this process remains unclear. "
- Thank you for this question! We will describe the data validation process in the next version of the paper. At a high level, we conducted two phases of dataset validation with our in-house Linguist team.
    - **Phase 1, Question and meta-label validation**. After the initial round of QA generation, an audit session was conducted, where expert annotators reviewed the question template, questions, and meta-labels (domain, question type, etc), applying edits as necessary with 2x human review (agreement rate 90%+). All problematic questions (e.g., a wrong false-premise question) were revised, and all conflicting labels were resolved by a third more experienced auditor. 
    - **Phase 2, Answer validation**. To ensure the answers in the benchmark are correct, we further conducted an auditing process for all answers.
        - For the web questions, an annotation team reviewed each question and conducted extensive search to make sure the answer is factually correct and includes comprehensive information (such as for set questions) with 2x human review (agreement rate 90%+). A third more experienced auditor then reviewed all conflicting answers and provided resolution. 
        - For the KG questions, a team of 5 engineers carefully checked the questions and queried the mock APIs manually to validate the answers are correct. This step resulted in ~5% answer correction.
        - In both of the above two steps,, we paid special attention to examples where the straightforward solutions output different answers from the ground truth answers, and asked the auditing team to double check those examples. This step yielded ~2% answer updates.

3. "The study does not report inter-annotator agreement for various metrics. This makes it difficult to assess the reliability of the annotations across various aspects of the benchmark, including question categorization, answer validation, and system response evaluation."
- We assessed the grading quality and inter-annotator agreement for both the data creation and manual evaluation processes. 
- For the data creation process, please see the data validation processes described above.  
- For the manual evaluation, we requested two human graders to grade each question (agreement rate ~94%), and when there is a conflict, a third more experienced grader (the reviewer) resolves it.

4. "Table 5 shows only marginal accuracy improvements when moving from LLM-only to Task 1 (adding web retrieval). This is concerning, and raises questions about the effectiveness of the retrieval process and the relevance of the retrieved information."
- A straight-forward RAG solution at best improving marginally over LLM-only is a common observation we have made over both CRAG and other internal benchmark datasets. There are multiple reasons:
    - Our straightforward solution uses web snippets to fill in a 4k size window to construct the prompt and truncate the rest of the retrieval contents. For ~40% questions the prompt contains the answer.
    - The web snippets also contains information that is not directly related to the question, and those information can lead to hallucinations in answer generation. Thus, the hallucination rate can be much higher (14% for LLM-only and 28% for Task 1 for GPT-4). 
- With that being said, the retrieval results are of reasonable quality. 
    - **Retrieval recall**: According to our latest recall analysis, for 93% of web questions and 74% of KG questions, the web search results contain the  ground truth facts. 
    - **Retrieval ranking**: We additionally plot the hit@k curve for retrieved web pages in Figure 1. It shows that hit@k grows sharply at the beginning, and flattens out later on, thus the ranking is healthy. 
    - **Top-5 coverage**: Top-5 web pages used in task 1 has reasonable coverage (70%), comparable to what we observed in practice when developing RAG systems. In addition, the non-perfect coverage allows us to test whether the RAG solutions admit "I don't know" when the retrieval results do not contain the necessary information, and allows jumps of quality for Task 2 and 3.
- Finally, we highlight that these results demonstrate the many challenges faced by RAG systems and serves the purpose of the CRAG benchmark. There is significant room for improvement beyond a straightforward RAG solution; indeed, we see much higher scores from KDD Cup competition teams (+20%)
- We will clarify the above points and update the recall results in the next version of the paper. 

5. "The sections above describe limitations. The authors have a very limited discussion of limitations." "The paper has a very limited discussion of related work, likely due to space constraints."
- We appreciate your constructive feedback and will include more discussions of limitations and related work in the revision.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions and comments! We are glad the reviewer finds "the diverse scenarios can allow fine-grained insights on system performance on different domains and question types"! Please see our detailed responses below:

1. "The authors make key contributions to evaluating RAG. The framework offers a good balance of difficulty and usability. It also allows insightful analyses of performance in different domains. My main concern is that the dataset maybe too small to be comprehensive, especially when evaluating domains separately. A discussion on comparative works and the current one in terms of size and diversity could be added." 
"- I suggest including the sizes of the other datasets in Table 1."
- Thank you for your comments. We have included the sizes of different benchmarks in Table 1. CRAG contains significantly more questions than 3 of the benchmarks. In comparison with the two larger datasets - MS MARCO and NQ, CRAG covers KG search, dynamic questions, and long-tail questions, which are essential for comprehensively evaluating the performance of RAG systems.
- Although the overall data size of 4409 is not a very large number, we made sure the majority categories contained a reasonable size to draw statistically significant conclusions. In particular, the granularity of data within each category enables us to achieve <5% margin of error at a 95% confidence level for most cases.  

| **Benchmark**            | Web retrieval | KG search | Mock API | Dynamic question | Torso and tail facts | Beyond Wikipedia | Size |
|--------------------------|---------------|-----------|----------|------------------|----------------------|------------------|------|
| **QALD-10**          | ❌            | ✅         | ❌       | ❌               | ❌                    | ❌               | 0.8K |
| **MS MARCO**        | ✅            | ❌         | ❌       | not explicitly   | not explicitly       | ✅               |  100K  |
| **Natural Questions** | ✅            | ❌         | ❌       | not explicitly   | not explicitly       | ❌               |  323K  | 
| **RGB**              | ✅            | ❌         | ❌       | ❌               | ❌                    | ✅               |  1K  |
| **FreshLLM**      | ❌            | ❌         | ❌       | ✅               | ❌                    | ✅               |  0.6K  |
| **CRAG**                 | ✅            | ✅         | ✅       | ✅               | ✅                    | ✅               |  4.4K  |

**Table 1**: Comparing CRAG to existing benchmarks for factual question answering.

2. "Additionally, the paper only discusses the results but should go further and offer guidance for readers on implications. I suggest the authors add a discussion based on the results guiding users of the benchmark on best models and pros and cons of the different retrieval systems tested."
- Due to the page limitation, our main text primarily focus on statistics of the benchmark (Table 3,4) and evaluation of different RAG solutions across various dimensions (Table 6, Figure 3, and Section 5), to highlight why the CRAG benchmark serves its purposes. We appreciate the reviewer's valuable suggestion and will include more discussions in the additional content page allowed for camera-ready if the submission is accepted.

title.value: A comprehensive dataset and useful benchmark for RAG

summary_and_contributions.value:
This work introduces a novel dataset for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with 4,409 Q&A pairs and mock API to simulate web and knowledge graph (KG) search.  The questions cover 5 domains: finance, sports, music, movies and open domain, and 8 question categories: questions with conditions, comparison, aggregation and multihop questions, set queries, post-processing heavy questions and false premise questions, as well as more straightforward questions asking for simple facts.  This dataset is aimed to provide a comprehensive and realistic questions to evaluate RAG models, and served as the basis for a KDD Cup 2024 Challenge. 

This work also provides an evaluation mechanism to test different components of a RAG system, namely web retrieval summarization, augmentation of web retrievals with calls to mock API of KGs, and end-to-end RAG using both web and API retrievals. The evaluation method distinguishes between hallucinated answers and missing answers. 

The final contribution is an evaluation of two instruction based LLMs (llama-3 Instruct and GPT-4 Turbo) and several industry SOTA RAG solutions, which reveal significant hallucination levels.

review.value: Overall, this is a much needed dataset addressing various gaps in the existing RAGs datasets and benchmarks. The diversity of the questions, tasks and external sources, as well as the ability to evaluate hallucination rates add a great deal of value to the research community.

strengths.value: The main strengths of this work are the comprehensive nature of the dataset, both in terms of the topics, types of questions, the external sources, i.e., mock web and KG APIs, types of tasks, and the evaluation metric differentiating between missing and hallucinated answers.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
This dataset is licensed for noncommerical use, which is suboptimal relative to some other RAG datasets, like FreshLLM, which seem to be licensed for commercial use (under the Apache license). 

I would have liked to see more open source models tested (the only open weights model evaluated is Llama 3 instruct).  

It was not clear whether the human annotator instructions have been released, as well as the prompts/instruction for automated evaluation, but it would be great to have all those instructions released as part of the dataset

Finally, no framework is provided to evaluate the effects of instruction fine-tuning or other type of fine-tuning of the RAG models. I would have liked to see more details about that potential direction (e.g., can the dataset be leverage for fine-tuning). 

Minor comments: 

*Section 1 refers to the 3 tasks as web retrieval, structured querying and summarization while Section 2 refers to them as retrieval summarization, KG and web retrieval augmentation and end-to-end RAG. It would be easier to follow the paper if the tasks are named consistently.

*For the closed models tested, I suggest providing the dates when the relevant API's were called.

limitations.value: I think the limitations have been adequately addressed in this work.

correctness.value: The dataset and the benchmarks seem to be constructed in a sound manner.

clarity.value: I think the paper is very clear and well written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Overall, the relation to other datasets relevant to RAG is adequately discussed.  I would have liked to understand how this benchmark is different from the RAG TREC (https://trec-rag.github.io) which uses modified MS Marco corpus.

documentation.value: The dataset is currently hosted on AICrowd and the authors state their intention to host it long-term in a Meta Research Github repo. In principle the Github (and AICrowd?) repos may be permanently deleted by Meta. Hosting the dataset in a permanent repository, like zenodo, would provide stronger assurances of long-term preservation.

title.value: A diverse and challenging benchmark for RAG.

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors propose CRAG, a dataset for benchmarking retrieval augmented generation. The dataset includes a diverse set of tasks across 5 different domains covering real user queries. Additionally, the authors also consider a diverse set of question types. The diverse scenarios can allow fine-grained insights on system performance on different domains and question types. The authors perform comprehensive evaluations for several straightforward RAG solutions. Finally, the authors design a framework for automatic evaluation system for quick iteration over different solutions.

review.value: The authors make key contributions to evaluating RAG. The framework offers a good balance of difficulty and usability. It also allows insightful analyses of performance in different domains. My main concern is that the dataset maybe too small to be comprehensive, especially when evaluating domains separately. A discussion on comparative works and the current one in terms of size and diversity could be added. Additionally, the paper only discusses the results but should go further and offer guidance for readers on implications. I suggest the authors add a discussion based on the results guiding users of the benchmark on best models and pros and cons of the different retrieval systems tested.

+ Results section looks comprehensive

title.value: Novel benchmark for modern RAG systems

summary_and_contributions.value: The CRAG benchmark introduces a comprehensive dataset for evaluating RAG systems, with more than 4000 question-answer pairs. These questions vary in their domain, question type, and temporal dynamics. The benchmark provides mock APIs for web and knowledge graph search, allowing for realistic testing of RAG capabilities. The paper presents a novel evaluation methodology, including a scoring system that penalizes hallucinations and an automatic evaluation method using LLMs. The paper evaluates both baseline LLMs as well as integrated RAG systems, and finds significant limitations in performance, particularly in handling dynamic information and complex reasoning tasks.

review.value:
The work addresses a significant gap in the field by providing one of the few RAG benchmarks specifically designed for modern LLMs.

Pros:

- The benchmark fills an important need in the evaluation of RAG systems.
- The benchmark covers diverse domains, question types, and temporal dynamics.
- By incorporating dynamic information, the benchmark provides a method for addressing data contamination.
- The use of full HTML pages and mock APIs closely mimics real-world RAG applications.
- The paper introduces a scoring system that penalizes hallucinations and presents an automatic evaluation method using LLMs, which shows high agreement with human evaluation.
- The evaluation reveals significant performance gaps in current RAG systems, particularly in handling dynamic information and complex reasoning tasks.

Cons:

- The benchmark uses a small retrieval candidate pool (up to 50 web pages per question), which may not adequately represent real-world retrieval challenges.
- The benchmark does not directly evaluate first-stage candidate pool construction, an important aspect of RAG systems.
- The paper lacks a clear description of the question/answer pair validation process.
- The absence of inter-annotator agreement reporting makes it difficult to assess the reliability of various benchmark aspects.
- The marginal improvements from LLM-only to Task 1 and the decreased performance on dynamic questions when using RAG are concerning.

Quality and Clarity:

The paper is generally well-structured and presents a clear motivation for the benchmark. The methodology for creating the dataset and the evaluation metrics are explained in detail. However, the lack of information on validation processes somewhat diminishes the overall quality of the work.

Originality:

CRAG represents a novel contribution to the field. The inclusion of temporal dynamics and entity popularity in the benchmark design is innovative.

Significance:

The significance of this work is substantial. RAG systems have become increasingly important over the last yer, so a comprehensive benchmark is crucial for progress in the field. 

However, the limitations raise questions about the benchmark's design.

strengths.value:
- The benchmark addresses a significant gap in the field by providing one of the few RAG benchmarks specifically designed for modern LLMs.

- CRAG appears to mitigate data contamination by including dynamic and recent information. This helps provide a more accurate assessment of LLM and RAG system capabilities.

- The benchmark covers a wide range of domains (Finance, Sports, Music, Movie, Open domain) and question types.

- The benchmark uses questions with varying levels of temporal dynamism, allowing for fine-grained evaluation of how RAG systems handle this issue.

- The benchmark tests systems' ability to handle both common and rare information requests.

- The use of full HTML pages and mock APIs simulates real applications of RAG systems.

- The paper presents a method for automatic evaluation of RAG responses, with high agreement with human evaluation. This allows for scalable evaluation of systems.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- The benchmark uses a small retrieval candidate pool (up to 50 web pages per question). It does not directly evaluate a first-stage candidate pool construction, which is a challenging retrieval task in its own right. The benchmark should be clearer that it is not providing an end-to-end evaluation of RAG systems, e.g. in situations where Google is not available.

- The paper lacks a clear description of the validation process for question/answer pairs. While some manual verification is mentioned, the methodology for this process remain unclear.

- The study does not report inter-annotator agreement for various metrics. This makes it difficult to assess the reliability of the annotations across various aspects of the benchmark, including question categorization, answer validation, and system response evaluation.

- Table 5 shows only marginal accuracy improvements when moving from LLM-only to Task 1 (adding web retrieval). This is concerning, and raises questions about the effectiveness of the retrieval process and the relevance of the retrieved information.

- Figure 2b shows that providing web and KG results actually decreases performance on real-time and fast-changing questions. This result suggests potential issues with either the RAG implementation, the quality of retrieved data, or the benchmark's design for handling dynamic information.

limitations.value: The sections above describe limitations. The authors have a very limited discussion of limitations.

correctness.value: See above for questions/concerns regarding validation of the benchmark and some surprising experimental results.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper has a very limited discussion of related work, likely due to space constraints.

documentation.value: The benchmark was used in the KDD Cup 2024 challenge, so it has already been distributed and publicly used on a large scale.

title.value: A new comprehensive RAG benchmark in the QA Setting

summary_and_contributions.value:
1. The creation of CRAG, a rich and comprehensive benchmark for evaluating RAG systems, including a diverse set of 4,409 QA pairs and mock APIs for web and KG search.
2. The design of three tasks to test different components of RAG solutions: web retrieval, structured querying, and summarization, with a focus on realistic use cases and dynamic question handling.
3. A comprehensive evaluation of both straightforward and state-of-the-art RAG solutions on CRAG, providing insights into their performance and revealing areas for improvement.

review.value: This paper is clearly written and easy to follow. RAG is an important task and is widely used in industry now. So it's quite meaningful to properly benchmark this task. This proposed dataset CRAG includes a wide array of questions that cover various domains and question types, reflecting real-world QA scenarios with a realistic distribution of entity popularity and temporal dynamism. And also CRAG cover a set of different question types, including set, comparison, multi-hop and etc.

strengths.value: CRAG addresses a current gap in RAG research by providing a robust platform to test and compare the latest solutions, thus facilitating progress in the field.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: CRAG only benchmark the generative model in the process, and leave the retrieval part not fully covered (Although end-to-end RAG task require the entire system), but it does not provide a way to benchmark the quality of the retriever.

limitations.value: The benchmark relies on static snapshots of data for evaluation, which may not fully account for the constantly changing nature of information, particularly for real-time and fast-changing facts.

correctness.value: The datasets are constructed in a sound way.

abstract.value: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has recently emerged as a promising solution to alleviate Large Language Model (LLM)’s deficiency in lack of knowledge. Existing RAG datasets, however, do not adequately represent the diverse and dynamic nature of real-world Question Answering (QA) tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Comprehensive RAG Benchmark (CRAG), a factual question answering benchmark of 4,409 question-answer pairs and mock APIs to simulate web and Knowledge Graph (KG) search. CRAG is designed to encapsulate a diverse array of questions across five domains and eight question categories, reflecting varied entity popularity from popular to long-tail, and temporal dynamisms ranging from years to seconds. Our evaluation on this benchmark highlights the gap to fully trustworthy QA. Whereas most advanced LLMs achieve $\le 34\%$ accuracy on CRAG, adding RAG in a straightforward manner improves the accuracy only to 44%. State-of-the-art industry RAG solutions only answer 63% questions without any hallucination. CRAG also reveals much lower accuracy in answering questions regarding facts with higher dynamism, lower popularity, or higher complexity, suggesting future research directions. The CRAG benchmark laid the groundwork for a KDD Cup 2024 challenge, attracted thousands of participants and submissions. We commit to maintaining CRAG to serve research communities in advancing RAG solutions and general QA solutions. CRAG is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/CRAG/.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
